name: Kokileswarar Temple, Tirukkozhambam
deity: Shiva as Kokileswarar (the lord worshipped by the cuckoo), with the goddess Soundara Nayaki
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram
period: Tevaram era, with Chola-period structure (Sembiyan Mahadevi patronage)
summary: Tirukkozhambam, near Kumbakonam, honours Shiva as Kokileswarar — the lord worshipped by the cuckoo — with the goddess Soundara Nayaki. A Paadal Petra Sthalam sung in the Tevaram and cared for by the Thiruvaduthurai Adheenam, the temple keeps two tender legends: a cursed being who, in the form of a kokila (cuckoo), worshipped the lord here and regained his nature; and Parvati, cursed to a cow's form, who worshipped here and whose hoofprints are shown on the lingam. The Chola queen Sembiyan Mahadevi is remembered as its patron.

sections.history: Tirukkozhambam, near Kumbakonam, is an ancient Shaiva village revered in the Tevaram and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. The old name of the place, Kokilapuram, carries its cuckoo legend. The stone temple is of the Chola period and is particularly associated with the great queen Sembiyan Mahadevi, a renowned patron of delta temples; the shrine is today administered by the Thiruvaduthurai Adheenam, one of the major Shaiva mutts.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Kokileswarar; the goddess Soundara Nayaki has her own shrine. Opposite the entrance lies the Brahma Theertham, a sacred tank. On the lingam, worshippers are shown the marks said to be the hoofprints of Parvati in her cow form, tying the temple's art directly to its legend.
sections.legends: Two legends give the temple its character. In one, a celestial being (in some tellings a Vidyadhara named Chandhan) was cursed and took the form of a kokila, a cuckoo; worshipping Shiva here for long, he regained his true nature, and the lord took the name Kokileswarar. In the other, Shiva and Vishnu played a game of dice with Parvati as judge; her ruling displeased Shiva, who cursed her to be born as a cow, and in that form she worshipped here, her hoof striking the ground to uncover the lingam — the marks remaining visible to this day.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam — with the observances of the Thiruvaduthurai Adheenam adding their own order. The goddess's legend gives the festivals of Parvati a special meaning here.
sections.experience: Tirukkozhambam offers the pilgrim two gentle stories of curse and redemption — a cuckoo and a cow who each found grace at the lord's feet. The darshan of Kokileswarar, the hoofprints on the lingam and the quiet patronage of a great Chola queen give the delta shrine a tender, storied depth.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirukkozhambam is near Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district, roughly 10 km away; Kumbakonam is the nearest rail head and town, with local buses and taxis to the village.
